text: When Jesus had finished saying all this in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum.
A centurion there had a servant whom he valued highly, and the man was sick and about to die.
When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent some elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and save his servant's life.
They came to Jesus and pleaded with him earnestly: "He deserves to have you do this for him,
for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue."
So Jesus went with them. He was not far from the house when the centurion sent friends to say to him: "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof.
That is why I did not consider myself worthy to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.
For I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I say to one, 'Go,' and he goes; and to another, 'Come,' and he comes; and to my servant, 'Do this,' and he does it."
When Jesus heard this, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him he said, "I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith."
And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.
Soon afterward Jesus went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a large crowd went along with him.
As he approached the town gate, there—a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. A large crowd from the town was with her.

versions.text: As he approached the town gate, a dead man was being carried out—the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. A large crowd from the town was with her.
versions.explanation: The vivid καὶ ἰδοὺ ("and behold") is dropped; restoring a marker of surprise preserves the narrative immediacy Luke intends and reads well aloud.

text: When the Lord saw her, his heart went out to her, and he said, "Do not weep."
Then he went up and touched the bier, and those carrying it stood still. He said, "Young man, I say to you, arise."
The dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him back to his mother.
Awe seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, "A great prophet has arisen among us," and, "God has visited his people."
And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country.
John's disciples told him about all these things. So John called two of them
and sent them to the Lord to ask, "Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?"
When the men came to him, they said, "John the Baptist sent us to you to ask, 'Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?'"
At that very time Jesus healed many people of diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits, and he gave sight to many who were blind.

So he answered them, "Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, those with leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have the good news preached to them.
And blessed is the one who is not offended by me."
After John's messengers had left, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: "What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?
What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Look, those who wear splendid clothes and live in luxury are found in royal palaces.

versions.text: What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? No, those who wear splendid clothing and live in luxury are in royal palaces.
versions.explanation: The word "No" is an addition not present in the Greek; ἰδοὺ is an attention-getting "look/behold" that also reads well aloud. Also, μαλακοῖς ἱματίοις is more precisely "soft clothing," which sets up the contrast with the "splendid clothing" of the next clause.

text: But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and far more than a prophet.
This is the one about whom it is written: 'Behold, I send my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way before you.'
I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than John; yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he."
(All the people who heard this, even the tax collectors, acknowledged God's justice, for they had been baptized with John's baptism.
But the Pharisees and the experts in the law rejected God's purpose for themselves, since they had not been baptized by him.)
"To what, then, shall I compare the people of this generation? What are they like?
They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling out to one another: 'We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.'
For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, 'He has a demon.'
The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say, 'Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.'
Yet wisdom is vindicated by all her children."
One of the Pharisees invited Jesus to eat with him, so he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at the table.
And a woman in that town who was a sinner learned that he was dining at the Pharisee's house. She brought an alabaster jar of perfume,
and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears. Then she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the perfume.
When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, "If this man were a prophet, he would know who is touching him and what kind of woman she is—that she is a sinner."
Jesus answered him, "Simon, I have something to tell you." "Tell me, Teacher," he said.
"Two men owed money to a certain lender. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.
Neither of them could pay, so he canceled the debts of both. Now which of them will love him more?"
Simon answered, "I suppose the one who was forgiven more." "You have judged rightly," Jesus said.

Then he turned toward the woman and said to Simon, "Do you see this woman? I came into your house. You gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.
You gave me no kiss, but from the moment I came in she has not stopped kissing my feet.
You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with perfume.
Therefore I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven—for she loved much. But the one who is forgiven little loves little."

versions.text: Therefore I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven—and so she has loved much. But the one who is forgiven little loves little."
versions.explanation: The Greek conjunction ὅτι introduces a reason or evidence clause ("because/for she loved much"). Rendering it "and so" reverses the direction of the clause and turns it into a consequence, which is an interpretive move not supported by the wording itself. A more literal rendering preserves the ambiguity; the surrounding parable already guides the reader to understand her love as evidence of forgiveness already received. A footnote could note that the love is the evidence, not the cause, of her forgiveness.

text: Then he said to her, "Your sins are forgiven."
The others reclining at the table began to say among themselves, "Who is this who even forgives sins?"

versions.text: The other guests began to say among themselves, "Who is this who even forgives sins?"
versions.explanation: συνανακείμενοι specifically means those reclining at table with him; making the setting explicit helps hearers picture the meal scene and reads smoothly aloud.

text: But he said to the woman, "Your faith has saved you. Go in peace."
